title: The clarinet wail of Rhapsody in Blue
hook: The most famous clarinet slide in music is said to have started as a joke in rehearsal.
peek: Rhapsody in Blue opens with a clarinet trill that swoops upward in a long, laughing wail. George Gershwin wrote a plain run of notes. The story goes that clarinettist Ross Gorman smeared it as a joke, and Gershwin told him to keep it.
lede: On 12 February 1924, at Aeolian Hall in New York, Paul Whiteman's band premiered George Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue. It opens with a single clarinet: a low trill, then a swooping rise of more than two octaves. That wail is now one of the best-known sounds in American music. As the usual story has it, it began as a joke.

bullets.text: In Gershwin's score, the opening was a trill followed by a quick scale of separate notes running up to the top. It was a flourish, but a tidy one, with each step written out.

In rehearsal, Whiteman's clarinettist Ross Gorman is said to have played the upper part as a continuous smear, sliding between the notes with a jazzy laugh. Gershwin liked it and asked him to do it that way in the concert.
A true slide is hard on a clarinet, which is built to jump between fixed notes. Players do it by slowly rolling their fingers off the holes while reshaping their mouth and throat to bend the pitch.
Later printed parts reflect the slide, and clarinettists now treat it as essential. Each player shapes it a little differently, so the opening few seconds say a lot about who is playing.
